claims.text: The starting material is a conventionally powder-metallurgy-processed CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy without h-BN.
The intervention is incorporation of 2–5 vol% nanoscale hexagonal boron nitride into CoCrFeNi during powder-metallurgy processing.
Preliminary thermal and chemical stability studies can guide processing modifications that improve h-BN dispersion and retention.
A uniform 2–5 vol% nanoscale h-BN dispersion will promote formation of a continuous lubricious tribofilm during sliding.
The tribofilm will remain effective from approximately 25 °C to 800 °C.
The structural mediator is a continuous h-BN-containing lubricious tribofilm formed in situ at the sliding interface.
The layered structure of h-BN facilitates low-resistance interlayer shear during sliding.
Interlayer shear enables h-BN to form a stable, self-adapting tribofilm.
The h-BN tribofilm acts as both a solid lubricant and a thermal barrier.
The tribofilm mitigates oxidation and wear.
Optimized processing will keep h-BN chemically and thermally stable over the full 25–800 °C range.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi has a coefficient of friction of approximately 0.3.
Unmodified CoCrFeNi has relatively high wear rates, particularly at extreme temperatures.
Adding h-BN will reduce the coefficient of friction from approximately 0.3 to approximately 0.1–0.15.
Adding h-BN will reduce wear relative to unmodified CoCrFeNi throughout the 25–800 °C range.
The friction and wear benefits will persist under high-load conditions at 800 °C.
The expected performance applies in ambient air or controlled atmospheres under representative pin-on-disk loads.
Aggressive corrosive atmospheres may cause deviations from the expected performance.
The long-term stability of the h-BN tribofilm under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading is uncertain.
Failure to obtain statistically significant friction or wear reduction, or failure to observe a stable continuous tribofilm at any tested temperature, would falsify the hypothesis.
